projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with John Espey was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: I retired in 1970 as a Lieutenant Colonel. I finished World War II when I was separated after World War II as a, as a staff sergeant.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: How did you get involved with getting enlisted or drafted?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: I was in college, and it was obvious to me that I was going to be drafted. So I joined the Army in June, 1942. And they not only was I recognized that that, that I was going to have to go in the military. Everybody else was. SO I knew that the time to, that was the time to go. It was at that time a possibility, looked like we might be defeated, and it was a thing to do.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: How did you personally feel about joining, being drafted?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Well, I kinda felt it was my responsibility. My father was a veteran of World War I, and my great-grandfather was a veteran of the Civil War. And several of my uncles and cousins were in World War I, and some cousins were already in World War, in the military in World War II. So I felt like it was my job to do, to serve.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: On joining, what were some of your earliest memories of like your training?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Well, I went to, when I went in, I went to Fort Ben Harrison in Indiana which is near Indianapolis, and is where I was inducted. And I went from there to took basic training at Camp Kroft, South Carolina, and I was there oh, on the order of... I took basic training, was there for three months. And I stayed there for the rest of the year. I worked, I was on cadre. And actually, I was doing training teaching people to do the same thing I just got through doing.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: What kind of things were you doing? What kind of training did you do?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Oh, just infantry training, rifle marksmanship, and small unit tactics, and how to take care of yourself, oh, health, taking care of your quarters and your equipment.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Did you mind the training?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Well, it wasn't exactly fun, but I knew I had to do it. And everybody else did it. So I felt like if they could do it, I could too.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: After your training, after you were past the basic training and everything, what was your next step?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: The next job, I stayed on for three cycles where I was on cadre and giving the training. I was promoted to Corporal and stayed there and gave training.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Where did you go after that?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: After that I went to an engineering school in Michigan. And from there, I went to the 76th Division which was Camp McCoy, Wisconsin. It was a combat division. And I, oh, I stayed there about a year, and the dates are kinda run together sometimes. And from there, I went to North Africa and to Italy.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Could you share with us some of your experiences in North Africa, what that was like?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Well, basically, we just got the, we arrived there, and there was no units to join. I'm not sure why we were, we ended up in North Africa. Apparently they needed the ships that we were on. And they moved the ships to, we ended up in a British tent camp. And I must say we were there for six to eight weeks. And then we went from there to Italy into Naples. And that, this was at roughly the time of the Battle of the Bulge, and apparently, there was a lot of turbulence in personnel, turbulence there. So we were formed, when we got to Italy, we were formed up in a provisional infantry company and took over a... there was a bay section stockade, and we were took over the security at the base section stockade. It was out at Descerta (?), and I went, we were there eight or nine months. And then, at that time the war in Europe was over, and we were processed to go back and join the unit and to make the invasion of Japan. However, when I got back the Unites States, the war in Japan was over in August of '45 I guess it was. The Japan War was over, and then I ended up working at a, the separation center at Camp Adelberry and later at Fort Knox.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: During your, when you separated and working at Fort Knox and all... ?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Well, I wasn't separated at that... I was, what I did we when the soldiers were coming back from Europe and Japan, they were being separated because I didn't have enough points to get separated. Then that was my just almost, oh, I guess you'd almost call it a clerical job. You were filling out forms and telling them you know what their rights were when they became, when they were discharged and checking to make sure they got their pay. I didn't make out the pay. Somebody else did that, but me and several hundred others guy, we'd get this pile of papers and sort it out and put it into some kind of form so the files would be correct. Then somebody else would type up a discharge, and it would be presented to the guys at the time that they were finished. Then of course, when my turn came to get discharged, why I went through the same process. But oh, I guess I worked there at the two places about eight or nine months. I can't, it all runs together. And of course, that happened a long time ago, '45.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Throughout your service, just though out the through everything, how was like the conditions of where you and the fears and all?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: From pretty bad to fairly good. You know, the military gets food for instance, very good. And if you got a good mess sergeant, and you got a good mess officer, the meals you get are good. But it's just like a restaurant. If you don't have good employees, the food's lousy you know?

Let me tell you a story about something that happened. Early in World War II. They realized there was going to be a possibility of the shortage of food you know. Civilians had rationing that they couldn't buy but so much sugar and so much meat and so forth. They had the ration system. But in the Army and same as the Navy and Marines, they tried to conserve food. And they found that a lot of soldiers were, had a tendency to, you'd go through the mess. And you know how a mess hall operates. You walk down a line, and they give you a spoonful of this and two spoonfuls of that on a metal tray is the way it worked. I don't think it works that way anymore, but anyway... So, people taking food, and they wouldn't eat all of it. A lot of people at that time, they weren't used to a lot of food. In my case for instance, I never had shrimp until I went to was in Washington, D.C. until I had shrimp. Of course, if they had served shrimp in the mess hall, I might not have eaten it, you know. And a lot of the guys had never eaten grapefruit, and people had, very much everybody was regional food. And if it wasn't quite a fit to what they were used to, they would throw it away. So the General who was in charge of procurement of food and serving it did this. He went through, he'd make an inspection, and he'd take regimental commander, the battalion commander, and the company commander and one or two other people with him. And he'd stand and watch people coming out, and they'd throw their food away. Well, he'd walk up to this before their food was there, and he'd reach down and grab a handful and eat it. And he said, "Now see, that food's good." And then he'd make every one of these other guys do the same thing. Now, this was not a pleasant experience but so everybody was afraid that he was going to come around again soon. So they had a sign that says take what you want, eat what you take. And that reduced considerably the amount of food wastage. I don't know how you'd feel about something, about having to grab a handful of food out of the garbage can, but I really wouldn't look forward to it.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Did you ever feel like there was a shortage of supplies?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Yeah. There was sometimes some, circumstances created supply shortages. You know, somebody was buying items in the United States, and they were, the items were having to be shipped all over the world to India, to Italy, out in the South Pacific. And sometime when the ship was sunk, you had a shortage. I'll give you an example. Turn it off and I'll give you an example. Your question about shortages. Let me give you an example of one that came to my attention. During World War II in Italy. Mrs. Roosevelt and several other ladies came over to make an inspection. Well, while they were there, one of the complaints that they got from the nurses and the whacks is that they didn't have sufficient toilet paper, and the soldiers had similar complaints, but because of sanitary reasons, the ladies had more requirement for toilet paper than the guys did. Well, when Mrs. Roosevelt got back, of course, she talked to the president, and she basically told him they weren't treating those gals over there right. So immediately he called up somebody in the war department and said, "Look. You've got to get more toilet paper over there for those gals." And the reason that they weren't getting sufficient toilet paper over there was because shipping was short, and you could fill a ship full of toilet paper. And basically, what you were doing was shipping air because and then it became, there was a study made of how to get more toilet paper over there because you didn't, you had a lot of bulk, but you didn't have any weight. So there was a study made of how it could be done to get the toilet paper over there. And the first they did was they just compressed the heck out of it, you know. You'd just put in something to compress it, and you got all the air out of it. Well, the problem with that is while it was at sea, it would take that moisture out. And when you got there, you couldn't unroll it. So they had to figure out a system to get it over there and it be useful when it got there. That's an example of a shortage. Of course, not having enough toilet paper would not cause the war effort to come to a halt, but it was a moral problem with the gals. And but if you, every ship that came over with toilet paper on it, you couldn't because of the shortage of shipping, you couldn't ship food and ammunition and repair parts and so forth.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: How was, you were talking about moral just now. How was the General where you were?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Uh, everybody bitched (laughing) But you know, everybody else was in the same shape that you were. So but it just, just the way it is. I mean you guys go to school. Are you happy every day? I bet, I bet I got the answer to that one right away.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Did you ever feel pressured or scared or nervous?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Oh yeah, a couple of times I felt scared.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: You could explain or elaborate?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Could you elaborate or share?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Well, here I was about 20 years old. I had a pack on my back and a rifle, and I was walking up a gang plank going on to a ship at Newport Harbor. First time I had ever been on a ship. First time I had ever been at sea. It was not one of my better moments. Nobody was shooting at us. Of course, there were submarines out on the east coast, and they sank a lot of ship tonnage out there. But nobody shot at us as far as I know in our convoy, but it was about 3:00 in the morning. And crawling up that long gangplank wasn't...

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: I can imagine. How long were you at sea at a time?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Oh, about nine days.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Did you have a lot of men or friends sick?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: I don't know how many...the ship was the U.S.S. Black as I remembered, and I don't have no idea of how many people were on it. We were all replacements. We were not part of any unit. We were just replacements.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: How did you keep in touch with your family?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Letters.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Letters. Was the mailing system and all that pretty good?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Uh, yeah. During the war, they had what they called V-mail. What happened, you'd write a letter on this form, and you'd mail. And it would go to a central place, and they'd make a photograph of it. And then that series of photographs would go to some central point in Europe or Italy or somewhere. And then they would make a picture of it, and that would be what you'd get as far as mail. You know, a letter on a normal piece of flimsy stationary would be useful to replace the toilet tissue we were talking about earlier, but one of these pictures would not be much help on that, (laughs) that circumstances.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: How did you all keep yourselves entertained? Like what entertain did you all have?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Uh, they had movies some times at night, maybe when you were back where they could have movies. And there was always card game and craps, crap games, and conversation and bull session. And course when you got leave, why, you know if you'd go into some of the... we went, of course we, Ed Lind went into some of the Italian towns. And some places, the special services had tours. While I was in, at Decerta and at the replacement depot outside of Naples. I had a chance, I went through Pompeii, and I went through that... of course it was essentially an archeological dig. You could, I talked to people who have been there since, and their description of it was the same as mine at that time. So you had all those things that you could do. Of course, there was always a bar where you might go and have a drink. Course in Italy, it was mostly Cognac and Chianti. At that time, Italians were extremely short of food. So there was very little chance of eating out. A couple of times, I, they had, you'd go in a bar, and they'd have something to eat. Fact is, they had, the first pizza I ever ate was in Italy. But the pizza they had then was just bread with tomato sauce and maybe some pepper or something on it. Not like you get from the pizza shops here.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: What did you do after you were discharged?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: I went back to school. I finished my degree.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: On the G.I. Bill?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Pardon?

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Did you go back to school under the G.I.Bill?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Yeah. Uh, as I mentioned that I was in a program where I went back every summer, I had to go back on active duty after. And I went during that time, I went to Fort Knox and Fort Meade and a couple of other places. I can't remember for sure.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Did you keep any contact with any of your friends?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Yeah, one guy whose I was with in Italy. He's 90 years old now. He's a dairyman in Wisconsin with his family, and I see him maybe once every other year, every year. Some years I haven't, but fact is I talked to his daughter recently. During the year, he's 90 years old, and he's got a turkey with a bow and arrow. And he shot a deer and caught a fish, a lake fish over 30 pounds at 90 years old. Pretty dang good, yeah. And I still hear from him. Another friend with us the period, Mike Donohue. I kept up with him the year he lived in Chicago, and his niece called me recently. And he had gone to a nursing home, and they said, I said he was at the point where he wouldn't be, where he wouldn't understand. So I guess I'd have to sort of say I still know him, but I don't, he doesn't know me I guess anymore.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Could I get you briefly to describe about how you personally felt about your service or the war?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Well, basically, the Army has been my life you know from when I was about 19 until I retired in '70. So I'm not going to perjure myself by telling you I enjoyed all of it. But I did enjoy a lot of it. I got to meet some good people. I met some people that weren't very good either. But 1 met some real nice people. You know, as 1 mentioned earlier, after the war, I served three tours in Japan and Okinawa, Vietnam, Korea. I spent three years in France. I had some trips in other places in Europe, Germany, and I've been to Greece, Spain, England. I've been to more places than most of your travel directors that have been. And I've spent some time in South America, Brazil.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Do you have any final stories or anything you want to add?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: I got a lot of stories, but I don't know if they would add to this.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Please go ahead...please go ahead.

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: Several of those stories in those two books that we discussed. I've got some stories, but I don't know that, well... I will tell you one. It sort of impressed me. As I mentioned in this provisional infantry company that was set up to guard this prison. Now this prison where we were stationed was not German or Italian P.O.W.'s. It was American people who were criminals, and they were Americans in these prisons. And during the time I was there, they had hangings. They hung six people three different, two different times, three at each time. And you know that I don't remember specific crimes that these people committed, but they were quite significant crimes: Rape, murder. One guy I do remember. He got mad at the people in his company, and he was a guard. And the Company was bivouwacked in sort of a valley, and he set up a 30 caliber machine gun and fired at his own company and killed seven or eight people in his own company. And they overcame him, and he was tried and was convicted and hung at the stockade. The Army like they do on everything have a system for hanging people. I'll describe it real briefly if you have any interest in it. They set up three gallows, three places to hang these people, and they brought them out in Army ambulances where the Red Cross had been painted out. And with each one of them was a Chaplain and two guards and the driver of the vehicle. They brought them out individually, put the rope around them, had a mask over them, and each one were hung separately. The way they did it. Each major unit in Italy sent us a senior N.C.O. and one or two goof-ups in the unit. Of course, the purpose of this was let the Goof-ups and the Senior N.C.O.'s see that if you screwed up bad enough, that the Army would in fact hang you. And they, these people were formed up in units, and just military formation. And around them in a square were M.P.'s facing the where they were hanging. And M.P.'s and this unit that I was with facing the other way, facing out a square around them. So everybody was in the square that was supposed to observe it. And as I say, they had a system for hanging. And of course, when all these guys went back to their unit, they read the court marshal orders, general court marshal orders that sentenced these people to hang. And the word got out that if you screwed up bad enough, they would in fact hang you.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Did that work? Did that work?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: I don't know whether it worked for everybody, but it sure toned my activities down (laughs). I got the word.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Well, thank you very much. If there is anything you'd like to add?

sp.speaker: John Espey
sp.p: I can't think of anything. I guess I am one of the few people that ever witnessed a military hanging. I don't think there have been any since World War II. It's a, I don't know whether it's an honor or not, but it's certainly something different. I have other stories, but I'm sure I don't have a story that someone else that you've talked to has something very similar. So I hope what I told is interesting and helps.

sp.speaker: Brand Cook
sp.p: Thank you very much [END OF INTERVIEW]
